subtitle: Recognize the weight navigators carry, including secondary traumatic stress and boundary strain, and set the personal and organizational supports that help the work last.
audience: A short course for cultural navigators and the people who supervise them. It is not a mental health assessment or treatment; anyone who is struggling should reach out to their Employee Assistance Program, a health care provider or someone they trust.

lessons.title: The weight navigators carry
objectives: Describe secondary traumatic stress and some of its common signs.
Recognize risk factors that fit navigation work, such as heavy caseloads and isolation.
Describe boundary strain: being expected to be available to a community at all hours.
Notice early signs in yourself or a colleague without labeling anyone.
lessons.teaching:
Navigators often hear hard stories: families in crisis, people afraid of the system, experiences of discrimination or loss. Many navigators serve their own community, so those stories can feel personal. The National Child Traumatic Stress Network describes secondary traumatic stress as "emotional duress that results when an individual hears about the firsthand trauma experiences of another."

The network's fact sheet lists signs such as hopelessness, avoiding the people you serve, anger and cynicism, trouble sleeping, chronic exhaustion and physical ailments. It also names risk factors, several of which fit navigation work closely: being highly empathetic, carrying a heavy caseload, being socially or organizationally isolated, having unresolved personal trauma and feeling unprepared because of too little training.

Navigators also face boundary strain. Community members may call at night or on weekends, stop them at the grocery store or a place of worship, or expect them to fix things they have no power over. Saying no can feel like letting down their own people. Over time, being always available can wear down even the most committed navigator.

Noticing early helps. These signs are common responses to hard work, not personal failings or diagnoses. If you see them in yourself, take them seriously. If you supervise a navigator, ask about the work and how it is landing, rather than labeling the person. A simple, private "How are you carrying all this?" can open the door.
lessons.keyPoint: Hearing hard stories, often from your own community, has a cost. Notice the signs early, in yourself and others, without labeling anyone.
lessons.example: Practice case: The navigator has been taking calls from community members late at night and on weekends for months. Lately they feel exhausted, short-tempered with families and dread checking their phone.
lessons.question: What would help most to start?
choices: Keep answering every call, since the community depends on them.
Stop answering community calls entirely, without telling anyone.
Talk with their supervisor about what they are noticing, and agree on hours, an after-hours message and where urgent calls should go.
feedback: The commitment is real, but this pace is not sustainable, and the signs suggest it is already taking a toll.
Pulling back is understandable, but doing it silently may leave families without a path for urgent needs and the navigator without support.
This names what is happening, gets support and sets boundaries that protect both the navigator and the families, with a clear path for urgent needs.
lessons.reflection: What helps you notice when work is starting to weigh on you? Who would you tell?
lessons.action: Write down one sign that tells you work is weighing on you, and one person you would talk to when you notice it.

check.question: What is secondary traumatic stress?
check.correct: Emotional distress that results from hearing about another person's firsthand trauma.
wrong: A diagnosis that means someone should stop doing navigation work.
Stress that only affects people who are new to the job.
check.feedback: The National Child Traumatic Stress Network describes it as emotional duress from hearing about others' trauma. It is a common response to the work, not a verdict on a person. The fact sheet notes that longer experience is protective, and that feeling unprepared because of too little training raises the risk.

lessons.title: Supports that help the work last
objectives: Name organizational supports that reduce secondary traumatic stress, such as balanced caseloads and supervision.
Name personal practices that help, such as rest, peer support and clear boundaries.
Use simple words to set a boundary with a community member kindly.
Know where to turn for confidential support.
lessons.teaching:
The most important supports come from the organization, not the individual. The National Child Traumatic Stress Network's fact sheet names organizational strategies such as a balanced caseload, flexible scheduling and ongoing skills training, alongside supervision and peer support. A navigator cannot self-care their way out of an impossible caseload. Supervisors and managers can change the conditions.

Good supervision includes time to talk about how the work is landing, not only what got done. Some programs use reflective supervision, where the supervisor helps the worker think through hard cases and their own reactions. Peer support helps too: other navigators understand the work in a way most colleagues cannot.

Personal practices matter as well. The fact sheet mentions exercise, good nutrition, rest and stress reduction, and having someone who checks in with you about your own self-care. Clear boundaries are part of this. A navigator might say, "I want to help with this. I'm off work now, so let's talk tomorrow at nine. If it's an emergency, call this number." Kind, clear words protect the relationship and the navigator.

Know where confidential support is. State employees and many other workers have an Employee Assistance Program. A health care provider, a faith leader or a trusted friend can also help. Reaching out is part of doing this work well for a long time, and it is a strength, not a weakness.
lessons.keyPoint: Organizations carry most of the responsibility: caseloads, schedules, training and supervision. Navigators add rest, peer support, clear boundaries and confidential help when they need it.
lessons.example: Practice case: The supervisor notices the navigator has become withdrawn in meetings and has missed several follow-ups, which is unlike them. The navigator's caseload has nearly doubled in three months.
lessons.question: What should the supervisor do first?
choices: Meet privately, say what they have noticed without labeling, ask how the navigator is doing and look together at the caseload and what support would help.
Address the missed follow-ups as a performance problem.
Tell the navigator to take care of themselves and leave it there.
feedback: This opens a caring, private conversation and addresses the conditions the supervisor controls, such as caseload and support.
The missed follow-ups matter, but treating them only as performance misses the likely cause: a caseload that doubled.
Encouraging self-care is kind, but it puts the whole burden on the navigator and leaves the doubled caseload in place.
lessons.reflection: Which support would make the biggest difference for you or your team right now: caseload, schedule, supervision, peers or rest?
lessons.action: Choose one boundary sentence you could use with a community member after hours, and one organizational change you would ask your supervisor for.

check.question: According to the National Child Traumatic Stress Network fact sheet, which is an organizational strategy against secondary traumatic stress?
check.correct: Creating a balanced caseload, along with flexible scheduling and ongoing training.
wrong: Asking staff to handle their stress on their own time.
Increasing caseloads so staff stay busy and distracted.
check.feedback: The fact sheet names balanced caseloads, flexible scheduling and ongoing skills training as organizational strategies, alongside supervision and individual self-care.

cards.back: Emotional distress from hearing about another person's firsthand trauma.
High empathy, heavy caseloads, isolation, unresolved personal trauma and too little training.
Being expected to be available to a community at all hours.
Balanced caseloads, flexible scheduling, ongoing training and supervision.
"I want to help. I'm off now, so let's talk tomorrow at nine. If it's an emergency, call this number."

aid.heading: Notice
items: Exhaustion, trouble sleeping, dread of the phone.
Hopelessness, cynicism or avoiding the people you serve.
Ask, privately: How are you carrying all this?

aid.heading: For supervisors
items: Check caseloads and spread them fairly.
Make time in supervision for how the work is landing.

aid.heading: For navigators
items: Set work hours and an after-hours message.
Agree where urgent calls should go.
Use your Employee Assistance Program or another trusted source of support.

sources.title: National Child Traumatic Stress Network — Secondary Traumatic Stress: A Fact Sheet for Child-Serving Professionals (2011)
sources.note: Defines secondary traumatic stress and lists signs, risk factors and individual and organizational strategies, including supervision, balanced caseloads, flexible scheduling, ongoing training, rest and a self-care accountability partner.

sources.title: C3 Project — Community Health Worker Roles and Scope of Practice (2018), as published by Wayne State University
sources.note: Lists cultural mediation, advocacy and outreach among community health worker roles, the kinds of work that bring navigators close to people's hardest experiences.
